title: Al-Kahf, part one
tomorrow: why would a wise man hole a poor family's boat?

cards: Finals week. Somebody in every group chat deletes their apps and announces cave mode. The Qur'an has a cave too, and the people in it are young.
A few young men in a city that pressed them to give up their faith slip out toward the hills. They have no plan past the mouth of a cave.
At the entrance they stop and pray, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! Give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight." Then they go in, and they sleep.

teach.h: YOUNG, WITH NOTHING, AT A CAVE.
teach.b: Al-Kahf tells it like a dream. The sun slides past the cave's mouth. Their dog lies with his paws stretched across the threshold.
When they wake, they guess they've slept a day, or part of one. One of them walks into town with their silver coin to buy food, and the world has moved on without them.

Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the surah lets people argue over how many sleepers there were, then sets the argument down. Only God knows their number, it says, so don't quarrel about it.
The count was never the point. The prayer at the door was.

teach.h: A MAN TOO SURE OF HIS GARDEN.
teach.b: Then, in the same reading, a second picture: a man with two gardens of vines and date palms and a stream between, so sure of them he can't imagine them ever perishing.
His friend answers: "If only, when thou enteredst thy garden, thou hadst said: That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah!"
Then the fruit is ruined, and he's left wringing his hands over everything he spent. Two pictures side by side.
Young men with nothing, who ask for mercy and are kept. A man with everything, who forgets whose strength it was.
The cave isn't a hideout. It's a place where you're held for a while, and from which you walk back out.
A report some scholars accept speaks of a light between two Fridays for whoever reads this surah, which is why some Muslims read it every Friday.

how: Some Muslims read Surah al-Kahf on Fridays, following a report about a light between two Fridays; it is read aloud in Arabic or quietly from a copy or a phone.

o: the Night Journey to Jerusalem and the heavens
the Mountain where Musa was given the law
the Cave: the surah of the sleepers and the gardens

games.q: who's who in the cave and the garden — tap the pairs.
p: prayed for mercy at the cave's mouth
carried to town to buy food
a man too sure they'd never perish

s: the surah settles exactly how many sleepers there were
it lets people guess, then says only God knows their number, so don't quarrel over it.
the young men asked for mercy before they slept
mercy from Thy presence, and right conduct in their plight (18:10).
the cave story is mainly about escaping the world
they're kept in the cave, and they wake and walk back into town.

games.q: your cousin's food truck is booming and he posts that nothing can stop him now. his friend wants to say something. what fits the garden story?
o: warn him the truck will fail, like the garden did.
remind him gently whose strength it is: what Allah wills.
tell him wealth itself is the problem and he should sell.
games.why: the friend in the story doesn't curse the garden or the money. he says what the owner forgot: that which Allah wills; there is no strength save in Allah.

practice: Say the young men's line out loud, slowly: our Lord, give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight. If it's your prayer, say it as one; if not, hear it as theirs.
Then let the sit be a cave: not a place to hide from your week, a place to be held in it.

wordCard.voice: Al-Kahf. The Cave: the surah of the sleepers and the two gardens, the one some Muslims read on Fridays.

orig.note: Arabic: the cave. the surah takes its name from the young men's refuge.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: the cave, a kept place with a door you walk back out of. Part one, read.
